questions.question: What characterizes supervised learning?
options: Training on examples with known target labels
Learning only through rewards from an environment
questions.explanation: Supervised learning maps inputs to labeled outputs.

questions.question: Predicting the selling price of a house is what type of task?
questions.explanation: The target is a continuous numeric value, which makes it regression.

questions.question: Which algorithm is an unsupervised clustering method?
questions.explanation: k-means groups unlabeled points into k clusters.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a held-out test set?
options: To increase the training set size
To estimate how the model performs on unseen data
questions.explanation: The test set is kept aside so its score approximates generalization performance.

questions.question: What is overfitting?
options: The model fits training data well but performs poorly on new data
The model performs poorly on both training and new data
The model has too few features
questions.explanation: An overfit model memorises noise in the training set and fails to generalize.

questions.question: In machine learning, what is a feature?
options: An input variable used to make predictions
questions.explanation: Features are the measurable input attributes the model learns from.

questions.question: How is classification accuracy calculated?
options: True positives divided by predicted positives
True positives divided by actual positives
Correct predictions divided by total predictions
questions.explanation: Accuracy is the fraction of all predictions that are correct.

questions.question: Despite its name, logistic regression is mainly used for which task?
questions.explanation: It models the probability of a class with the logistic function.

questions.question: Which formula defines precision?
questions.explanation: Precision is the share of predicted positives that are actually positive.

questions.question: What does k-fold cross-validation do?
options: Trains k different algorithms and picks the best
Splits data into k parts and uses each part once as validation while training on the rest
Repeats training k times on the full dataset
questions.explanation: Averaging over k validation folds gives a more stable performance estimate.

questions.question: Which regularization technique can shrink some coefficients exactly to zero?
questions.explanation: The L1 penalty's geometry produces sparse solutions, performing feature selection.

questions.question: For which algorithm is feature scaling most important?
questions.explanation: k-NN uses distances, so features with large ranges dominate unless scaled; tree splits are scale-invariant.

questions.question: A model with high bias and low variance is most likely to be:
questions.explanation: High bias means the model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern.

questions.question: A classifier has TP=40, FP=10, FN=20, TN=30. What is its recall?
questions.explanation: Recall = TP/(TP+FN) = 40/60 ≈ 0.67 (0.80 is precision, 0.70 is accuracy).

questions.question: What can happen if the learning rate in gradient descent is too large?
options: Training always converges faster to the exact minimum
Updates overshoot the minimum and the loss may diverge
questions.explanation: Too large a step jumps past the minimum and can make the loss oscillate or grow.

questions.question: How does a random forest build its ensemble?
options: Trains trees sequentially, each correcting the previous one's errors
Trains a single very deep tree
Clusters the data and fits a tree per cluster
Trains many decision trees on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets and combines their votes
questions.explanation: Bagging plus random feature selection decorrelates the trees and reduces variance.

questions.question: Which practice introduces data leakage?
options: Fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting into train and test
Fitting a scaler on the training set only
questions.explanation: The scaler then learns statistics from test data, leaking information into training.

questions.question: What does a ROC AUC of 0.5 indicate?
options: The model ranks positives no better than random guessing
The model predicts positives half the time
questions.explanation: AUC is the probability a random positive is ranked above a random negative; 0.5 is chance.

questions.question: On a dataset with 99% negatives, why is accuracy a poor metric?
options: Accuracy cannot be computed on imbalanced data
Accuracy always equals recall on imbalanced data
Predicting all negatives scores 99% accuracy while missing every positive
Accuracy penalizes false negatives too heavily
questions.explanation: Metrics like precision, recall, F1 or PR-AUC better reflect minority-class performance.

questions.question: How does boosting differ from bagging?
options: Boosting uses only one model; bagging uses many
Boosting is unsupervised; bagging is supervised
Boosting averages bootstrap models; bagging reweights errors
Boosting trains models sequentially, each focusing on previous errors; bagging trains them independently
questions.explanation: Boosting mainly reduces bias by sequential correction; bagging mainly reduces variance.

questions.question: What does Principal Component Analysis (PCA) find?
options: Orthogonal directions that capture maximum variance in the data
The most predictive features for a target label
questions.explanation: PCA projects data onto uncorrelated components ordered by explained variance.

questions.question: In k-NN classification, what usually happens as k increases?
options: The decision boundary becomes smoother: variance falls and bias rises
questions.explanation: Averaging over more neighbours smooths predictions, trading variance for bias.
